extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and early-career researchers writing mathematical research papers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting, revising, and deciding what to keep or discard when producing mathematical research papers; focuses on when to abandon, rewrite, prune, and learn from failed work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that not every idea succeeds
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not every idea leads to a success, and not every first draft forms a good template for the final draft."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize failure as a normal part of research and writing; do not treat every first draft as a near-final product. Avoid over-investing emotionally or temporally in early versions that are unlikely to survive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when to abandon projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes work must be "scaled down, refocused, or shelved altogether."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate projects pragmatically and be willing to discontinue or postpone them when they become unproductive. Options include scaling down scope, refocusing aims, or shelving the project to avoid wasting time on dead ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove non-essential elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemmas or sections that don't strengthen the paper should be "reluctantly jettisoned or deferred to another paper."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prune material that does not directly support the main narrative or results. Defer tangential results to separate work rather than bloating the current paper; reluctant removal is preferable to retaining irrelevant content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite completely when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers may require entire rewrites when "the structure of a half-written paper is clearly not optimal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to toss and rebuild large portions of a manuscript if the organization, exposition, or logical flow is poor. Partial edits may be insufficient when structural problems exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance persistence with pragmatism
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand when to persevere versus when to abandon "dead ends" that waste time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain persistence on promising directions but exercise pragmatic judgment to stop or redirect efforts that are unlikely to yield results. Weigh potential payoff against time and opportunity cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain quality standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing work should meet your expected quality level; not every piece should be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold manuscripts to personal (and field) standards for clarity, correctness, and significance. It's acceptable to keep some work private or unpublished if it does not meet those standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Back up everything
rubrics_metrics.description: Always backup work before major revisions; salvageable material may resurface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use versioning/backups so removed or shelved material can be retrieved later. Backups protect against irreversible loss during large rewrites and allow recovery of useful fragments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from failed work
rubrics_metrics.description: Even unsuccessful projects stored privately teach you "the limitations of your own tools."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat failed or abandoned projects as a source of insight about methods, techniques, and personal limitations. Review them to improve future problem selection and methodological choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing and pruning define 'good math'
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece of mathematical writing is "good" partly because of what it does not contain — what was thrown away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: View careful editing and the willingness to discard material as central to producing high-quality mathematics. Good exposition often results from rigorous pruning and selection, not merely from initial discovery.
